An Ice Storm Warning is triggered by ice accretion meeting or exceeding locally or regionally defined warning criteria, which is typically 1/4 inch or more of ice accumulation on an elevated horizontal flat surface [NWSI-10-513, section App-B, p. 35], [NWSI-10-1605, section App-A-26, pp. 61-62]. 

Because exact warning thresholds are set by each local National Weather Service office, specific criteria can vary by region [NWSI-10-513, section App-B, p. 35], [NWSI-10-1605, section App-A-26, pp. 61-62].

A Winter Storm Warning can be issued for three types of events [NWSI-10-513, section 6.3, p. 7]:

1. **Singular Event:** Snow, lake-effect snow (at regional discretion), ice, or sleet meeting or exceeding locally defined event-based warning criteria [NWSI-10-513, section 6.3, p. 7].
2. **Multiple Event:** A combination of snow, ice, sleet, and/or blowing snow where at least one of the precipitation elements meets or exceeds locally defined warning criteria [NWSI-10-513, section 6.3, p. 7].
3. **Impact Driven:** A winter storm is forecast, but expected accumulations will not meet traditional criteria [NWSI-10-513, section 6.3, p. 7].

*Note: Specific numerical thresholds (such as snow or ice amounts) are defined locally and regionally by each NWS office [NWSI-10-513, section App-D, pp. 41-42].*

The National Weather Service issues a Winter Weather Advisory for hazardous winter conditions that may cause significant inconveniences, but—if caution is not exercised—can lead to life-threatening situations [NWSI-10-513, section App-B, p. 35]. 

Specific criteria are set regionally and locally [NWSI-10-513, section App-D, pp. 41-42]. For example, in the Eastern and Pacific Regions, advisories are issued for falling snow accumulating up to 6 inches in a 24-hour period, or for thin icing on roads and structures up to 1/4 inch thick [NWSI-10-513, section App-E, pp. 43-44]. 

Because exact threshold criteria vary by local NWS office, check with your local forecast office for the specific criteria in your county.

Snow Squall Warnings are issued to provide advance notice of intense, short-duration periods of moderate to heavy snowfall accompanied by gusty surface winds that result in rapidly reduced visibilities and whiteout conditions [NWSI-10-513, section 7, p. 19]. 

Forecasters issue them when there are radar, satellite, or reliable reports of snow squalls meeting either of these conditions:
* **Condition 1:** Visibility of 1/4 mile or less in snow with sub-freezing ambient road temperatures [NWSI-10-513, section 7.2.1, p. 19].
* **Condition 2:** Plunging temperatures capable of producing flash freezes, combined with a significant reduction in visibility from falling and/or blowing snow [NWSI-10-513, section 7.2.1, p. 19].

National Weather Service Weather Forecast Offices should issue a Snow Squall Warning (SQW) when there is radar, satellite, or reliable observational evidence (such as from Departments of Transportation, webcams, or road networks) indicating snow squalls meeting or exceeding one or both of these conditions [NWSI-10-513, section 7.2.1, p. 19]:

* **Condition 1:** Visibility of 1/4 statute mile or less in snow, combined with sub-freezing ambient road temperatures [NWSI-10-513, section 7.2.1, p. 19].
* **Condition 2:** Plunging temperatures sufficient to cause flash freezes, along with a significant reduction in visibility from falling and/or blowing snow [NWSI-10-513, section 7.2.1, p. 19].

Forecasters also use their judgment regarding societal factors such as the time of day and day of the week, and may issue a Special Weather Statement (SPS) instead if lesser impacts are expected [NWSI-10-513, section 7.2.1, p. 19].

Forecasters are also encouraged to collaborate watch issuances for lower probabilities when local impact criteria warrant earlier messaging, and to issue them with as much lead time as possible when confidence is high, while balancing the need to inform the public against issuing too many false alarms [NWSI-10-513, section 6.3.2, p. 8].

The Winter Storm Severity Index (WSSI) produces five levels of impact: **Winter Weather Area**, **Minor Impacts**, **Moderate Impacts**, **Major Impacts**, and **Extreme Impacts** [NWSI-10-514, section 5.3.1, pp. 16-17].

A wind chill of -20°F will cause frostbite in just 30 minutes [WinterStorms-2008, p. 5]. 

The signs of frostbite include:
* A loss of feeling [WinterStorms-2008, p. 5]
* A white or pale appearance in extremities, such as the fingers, toes, earlobes, or tip of the nose [WinterStorms-2008, p. 5]

Hypothermia is a life-threatening condition that occurs when the body temperature drops below 95°F [WinterStorms-2008, p. 5]. 

Its warning signs include:
* Uncontrollable shivering [WinterStorms-2008, p. 5]
* Memory loss, disorientation, and incoherence [WinterStorms-2008, p. 5]
* Slurred speech [WinterStorms-2008, p. 5]
* Drowsiness and apparent exhaustion [WinterStorms-2008, p. 5]

If medical care is not available, warm the person slowly, starting with the body core (warming the arms and legs first can drive cold blood toward the heart and lead to heart failure) [WinterStorms-2008, p. 5]. You can use your own body heat to help [WinterStorms-2008, p. 5]. Get the person into dry clothing and wrap them in a warm blanket that covers the head and neck [WinterStorms-2008, p. 5]. 

Do not give the person alcohol, drugs, coffee, or any hot beverage or food; warm broth should be the first food offered [WinterStorms-2008, p. 5].

If you are stranded in a vehicle during a winter storm, you should:

* **Stay in the vehicle** to avoid becoming quickly disoriented in wind-driven snow and cold [WinterStorms-2008, p. 11].
* **Run the motor about 10 minutes each hour** for heat [WinterStorms-2008, p. 11].
* **Open a window a little** for fresh air to prevent carbon monoxide poisoning, and ensure the exhaust pipe is not blocked [WinterStorms-2008, p. 11].
* **Make yourself visible to rescuers** by turning on the dome light at night when running the engine, tying a colored cloth (preferably red) to your antenna or door, and—after the snow stops falling—raising the hood [WinterStorms-2008, p. 11].
* **Exercise periodically** by moving your arms, legs, fingers, and toes vigorously to keep blood circulating and stay warm, while avoiding overexertion [WinterStorms-2008, p. 11].
